Illumination in Rational Billiards

Amit Wolecki
Abstract

We show that for a rational polygonal billiard, the set of pairs of points that do not illuminate each other (not connected by a billiard trajectory) is finite, and use the same method to extend the results of [LMW16] and [AW17] about the number of pairs of points that are finitely blocked from each other with a certain blocking cardinality. We rely on previous work about the blocking property in translation surfaces which ultimately stems from results of Eskin, Mirzakhani and Mohammadi on dynamics of moduli spaces of translation surfaces.

1 Introduction

Consider a source of light as a point in a bounded planar region. The emanating rays hit the boundary and reflect with angle of reflection that equals the angle of incidence, angles taken between the rays and the tangent to the boundary at the point of incidence. Does such a light source illuminate the whole region? Is the region illuminable from any point? These two questions of planar geometry are attributed to Ernst Straus in the 1950s, although the requirement that the region is polygonal might have appeared later. An example for a region that is not illuminable by any point was given by Penrose [Pen58] in 1958 for a region with curved boundary. A set of examples for polygonal regions with two points that do not illuminate each other was given in the 1990s by Tokarsky [Tok95]. Those polygons have the property of being rational in the following sense:

Definition 1.1.

A polygon is called rational if all angles between edges are in ℚ​π\mathbb{Q}\pi where the angle between two edges is the angle at the intersection point of their linear continuation.

We use the language of billiard dynamical systems to discuss illumination. A pair of points on a polygon QQ do not illuminate each other if there is no billiard trajectory on QQ connecting those points. We consider trajectories between interior points or edge points that are not vertices and assume that billiard trajectories stop upon hitting a vertex. When QQ is rational, the process (which will be discussed in detail below) of unfolding QQ results in an associated translation surface MM. Illumination in rational polygons is then generalized by a restrictive condition defined for billiard trajectories as well as translation surface geodesics, called the blocking property. A pair of points A,B∈QA,B\in Q is finitely blocked if all billiard trajectories between them pass through some finite set, called a blocking set. The blocking set is not allowed to contain AA and BB. We denote the minimal cardinality of a blocking set for A,BA,B as B​C​(A,B)BC(A,B). Similarly, blocking and illumination is defined on MM: a pair x,y∈Mx,y\in M of non-singular points is finitely blocked if all geodesic trajectories on MM connecting xx and yy pass through some finite set disjoint from {x,y}\{x,y\}. Here we assume that geodesics are not continued through singular points, and discuss continuation through removable singular points later on. The terms blocking set and blocking cardinality are defined similarly, and B​C​(x,y)=0BC(x,y)=0 amounts to non-illumination of xx and yy. The illuminability or blocking of vertices in the billiard or singularities of the surface are not considered in the main results of this paper. However, as the set of pairs of such is finite, including vertices or singularities in the definition of illumination or blocking does not change the main results presented here. Also note that illumination and blocking are properties of translation surfaces in general, regardless of whether they are an unfolding of a rational billiard. Lelièvre, Monteil and Weiss [LMW16] had several results regarding translation surfaces in general: they showed that a translation surface MM is a ramified translation cover of the torus if and only if all pairs of non-singular points are finitely blocked from each other and in that case there is a typical nn such that every pair of points has B​C≤nBC\leq n. They also showed that for a fixed x∈Mx\in M, the set of points that do not illuminate xx is finite. For a rational polygon QQ that unfolds to a translation surface that is not a torus cover, Apisa and Wright [AW17] showed that if all angles are multiples of π/2\pi/2 then each point in QQ is finitely blocked from only finitely many other points, and in case there is an angle that is not a multiple of π/2\pi/2, then there are at most finitely many pairs of points that are finitely blocked.

Theorem 1.2.

Let QQ be a rational polygon with connected interior and let MM the translation surface obtained by unfolding QQ, then:

  1. (i)

    Only finitely many pairs of points in QQ do not illuminate each other.

  2. (ii)

    {(A,B)∈Q2:B​C​(A,B)≤n}\{(A,B)\in Q^{2}:BC(A,B)\leq n\} is finite for every integer n>0n>0 if and only if MM is not a torus cover.

Theorem 1.2(ii) extends the results of [LMW16] and [AW17] about the possible cardinality of finitely blocked pairs of points in the non-torus cover case, while the result in [LMW16] grants the ”only if” direction. It is concluded in [LMW16] that for a rational polygon QQ and a fixed A∈QA\in Q, there are at most finitely many points that do not illuminate AA. Theorem 1.2(i) extends this result in that the total amount of pairs of points that do not illuminate each other is finite (regardless of whether the unfolded surface is a torus cover or not). The results of [LMW16] and [AW17] rely on work of Eskin, Mirzakhani and Mohammadi [EMM], applied to the moduli spaces of translation surfaces to describe sets of interest (i.e, subsets of finitely blocked pairs) as submanifolds that locally are complex linear manifolds defined over ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Note that the statements in Theorem 1.2 do not necessarily hold when substituting QQ with MM. Hubert, Schmoll and Troubetzkoy ([HST08] §8) have constructed an example of a non-torus cover translation surface that has infinitely many pairs of points that do not illuminate each other. For other examples see [LMW16] §6.3.

Central to our discussion is the effect of the action of a dihedral group on a translation surface, defined when the surface is an unfolding of a rational polygon. Our results are thus relevant to translation surfaces arising from polygons, but not to arbitrary translation surfaces. One of the polygonal examples presented in [Tok95] was notable for being a rational polygon with two non-illuminable points, at the time of its discovery it had the fewest number of edges - 2626, compared to other polygonal examples with larger numbers of edges. Castro [Cas97] later presented an example with 2424 edges (published as a Quantum Magazine reader’s feedback, in response to an article about Tokarsky’s result on the illumination problem), and as a digestif for this paper we exhibit a more efficient example with 2222 edges and justify the following:

Theorem 1.3.

The minimal number of edges of a polygon with at least one pair of points that do not illuminate each other is at most 2222.

The mentioned examples for non-illumination rely on Tokarsky’s main lemma, which we reprove and extend in Lemma 3.1 to apply to a wider family of examples.

2 Illumination and Blocking in Rational Billiards and Translation Surfaces

Let Γ\Gamma be the group generated by the linear parts of reflections along edges of a polygon QQ. Γ\Gamma is finite if and only if QQ is rational and in this case a process of unfolding (also named Katok-Zemliakov construction) yields a translation surface MM: a compact, orientable surface with an atlas of planar charts (from open subsets of M∖ΣM\setminus\Sigma to ℂ\mathbb{C}) such that all transition maps are translations, and equipped with a flat metric defined outside a finite set of singularities Σ\Sigma. For a general description of translation surfaces we refer to [MT02], [Vor96]. Also note that Γ\Gamma can be defined for a general polygon, and finite Γ\Gamma is commonly the definition of a rational polygon [MT02], [Vor96]. The unfolding process begins with taking all reflections and rotations of QQ by elements of Γ\Gamma with arbitrary translations to avoid overlaps, marking the resulting set of polygons {Q(γ):γ∈Γ}\{Q_{(\gamma)}:\gamma\in\Gamma\} and denoting the affine maps ϕγ​(x)=γ​x+vγ\phi_{\gamma}(x)=\gamma x+v_{\gamma} for suitable vγ∈ℝ2v_{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} such that ϕγ​(Q)=Q(γ)\phi_{\gamma}(Q)=Q_{(\gamma)}. We then identify edges in the following way: edges e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} on Q(γ1),Q(γ2)Q_{(\gamma_{1})},Q_{(\gamma_{2})} respectively are glued by translations whenever (1) they correspond to the same edge in QQ, that is ϕγ1−1​(e1)=ϕγ2−1​(e2)\phi^{-1}_{\gamma_{1}}(e_{1})=\phi^{-1}_{\gamma_{2}}(e_{2}) and (2) e1e_{1} is parallel to e2e_{2} and γ1=τ​γ2\gamma_{1}=\tau\gamma_{2} where τ\tau is the derivative of reflection in e1e_{1}. For a more detailed description of this unfolding construction we refer to [Vor96] §2.2. The following lemma is a standard claim in billiards and we leave the proof to the reader.

Lemma 2.1.

Let QQ be a rational polygon and let MM be its unfolding. Let A,B∈QA,B\in Q a pair of distinct points that are not vertices of QQ, and E⊂Q∖{A,B}E\subset Q\setminus\{A,B\}. A billiard trajectory on Q∖EQ\setminus E connecting AA and BB exists if and only if there exists a geodesic line on M∖(π−1​(E)∪Σ)M\setminus(\pi^{-1}(E)\cup\Sigma) connecting a point in π−1​(A)\pi^{-1}(A) to a point in π−1​(B)\pi^{-1}(B) where π:M→Q\pi:M\rightarrow Q is the natural projection that maps x∈Mx\in M to a point in QQ that unfolds to xx.

Remark 2.2.

(Illumination and removable singularities.) Traditionally, a billiard trajectory is defined such that it stops upon hitting a vertex. When the billiard has a vertex with interior angle π/n\pi/n, the billiard flow can be continued to pass through this vertex. The continuation of a billiard trajectory α⁡(t)\alpha(t) through a π/n\pi/n vertex at time t0t_{0} amounts to the trajectory bouncing back on itself, i.e. α⁡(t0+t)=α⁡(t0−t)\alpha(t_{0}+t)=\alpha(t_{0}-t) for all tt. A vertex with interior angle π/n\pi/n is lifted to a removable singular point in the unfolded surface, on which the flat metric can be defined. A lifted trajectory α~​(t)\widetilde{\alpha}(t) allowed through the removable singularity at α~​(t0)\widetilde{\alpha}(t_{0}) would pass from one copy of the polygon to the copy shifted by a non-trivial element γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma such that α~​(t0+t)=γ​α~​(t0−t)\widetilde{\alpha}(t_{0}+t)=\gamma\widetilde{\alpha}(t_{0}-t) for all tt. The assertion in Lemma 2.1 holds for billiard and geodesic flows continued through π/n\pi/n vertices and removable singularities respectively. Yet in the general illumination question there is a slight difference between billiards and surfaces. A pair of points A,B∈QA,B\in Q that do not illuminate each other in the traditional billiard flow would still not illuminate each other if trajectories are allowed to continue through π/n\pi/n vertices. However on the unfolded surface we can consider a case where a pair of points in MM illuminate each other only when a singularity is removed, these points must descend to the same point in the billiard table QQ.

Lemma 2.3.

Let QQ be a rational polygon, A,B∈QA,B\in Q. The following are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    AA and BB are finitely blocked

  2. 2.

    xx and yy are finitely blocked for all x∈π−1​(A)x\in\pi^{-1}(A) and y∈π−1​(B)y\in\pi^{-1}(B).

In addition, for all n≥0,x∈π−1​(A),y∈π−1​(B)n\geq 0,x\in\pi^{-1}(A),y\in\pi^{-1}(B):

B​C​(A,B)≤n⇒B​C​(x,y)≤|Γ|​nBC(A,B)\leq n\Rightarrow BC(x,y)\leq|\Gamma|n (1)

Lemma 2.4.

Let n≥0n\geq 0, the set of lifted pairs of blocked points {(x,y)∈(M∖Σ)2:B​C​(π⁡(x),π⁡(y))≤n}\{(x,y)\in(M\setminus\Sigma)^{2}:BC(\pi(x),\pi(y))\leq n\} is invariant under the action of the product group Γ2\Gamma^{2}.

Proof.

For x∈Mx\in M nonsingular and γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma we have that γ​x\gamma x is nonsingular and π⁡(γ​x)=π⁡(x)\pi(\gamma x)=\pi(x) by construction as MM is defined by gluing copies of QQ that correspond to transformations by elements of Γ\Gamma. Observing the action of the product group, we can say that for every x,y∈Mx,y\in M nonsingular points γ1,γ2∈Γ\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}\in\Gamma we have B​C​(π⁡(x),π⁡(y))≤n⇒B​C​(π⁡(γ1​x),π⁡(γ2​y))≤nBC(\pi(x),\pi(y))\leq n\Rightarrow BC(\pi(\gamma_{1}x),\pi(\gamma_{2}y))\leq n which yields the invariance. ∎

Definition 2.5.

Let QQ a rational polygon with connected interior, and let MM the translation surface obtained by unfolding QQ. We denote the set of pairs of points on QQ that are blocked with blocking cardinality nn as 𝒬n​=def​{(A,B)∈Q2:B​C​(A,B)≤n}\mathcal{Q}_{n}\overset{\textup{{def}}}{=}\{(A,B)\in Q^{2}:BC(A,B)\leq n\}. The set of pairs of points blocked with blocking cardinality nn on the translation surface is denoted ℳn​=def​{(x,y)∈M^2:B​C​(x,y)≤n}\mathcal{M}_{n}\overset{\textup{{def}}}{=}\{(x,y)\in\widehat{M}^{2}:BC(x,y)\leq n\} where M^2​=def​(M∖Σ)2\widehat{M}^{2}\overset{\textup{{def}}}{=}(M\setminus\Sigma)^{2}.

For a general translation surface MM we treat the product M^2\widehat{M}^{2} as a translation structure with charts in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}, that are induced naturally by the charts of M∖ΣM\setminus\Sigma. It is shown in [LMW16] that MM is a branched cover of the torus if and only if there is some k>0k>0 for which ℳk=M^2\mathcal{M}_{k}=\widehat{M}^{2}. More details on ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} in case it is a proper subset of M^2\widehat{M}^{2} are provided in [LMW16] and also recalled in Proposition 2.7, describing it as a finite union of linear submanifolds of M^2\widehat{M}^{2}. Note that the real dimension of the complex submanifolds of M^2\widehat{M}^{2} is considered. A 22-dimensional linear submanifold S⊂M^2S\subset\widehat{M}^{2} can be locally defined by affine equations a​x+b​y=uax+by=u with xx and yy in the complex coordinates of MM, a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R} and u∈ℂu\in\mathbb{C} corresponding to the translation charts of SS. If SS is connected, the coefficients in these affine equations are constant through the charts. Note that SS respects the translation structure of M^2\widehat{M}^{2}.

Definition 2.6.

When SS is a connected 22-dimensional linear submanifold of M^2\widehat{M}^{2} that forms a compact and orientable surface, locally defined by affine equations of the form a​x+b​y=uax+by=u as described above, such that both real linear coefficients are nonzero, we call SS a translation surface affinely embedded in M^2\widehat{M}^{2}.

Proposition 2.7 (Lelièvre, Monteil, Weiss [LMW16], Theorem 2 and Theorem 11).

For a translation surface MM and an integer k≥0k\geq 0, the set ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} either equals M^2\widehat{M}^{2} or is a finite union of 00-manifolds, and 22-dimensional linear submanifolds of M^2\widehat{M}^{2} of the following kinds:

  1. 1.

    F×MF\times M or M×FM\times F for a finite F⊂MF\subset M.

  2. 2.

    A translation surface affinely embedded in M^2\widehat{M}^{2}.

Remark 2.8.

Proposition 2.7 holds for blocking in general translation surfaces and the proof in [LMW16] relies on a result by Eskin, Mirzakhani and Mohammadi describing orbit closures of the S​L​(2,ℝ)SL(2,\mathbb{R}) action on moduli spaces of translation surfaces. An orbit closure appears as a submanifold of the moduli space with an atlas of charts where each chart’s image is an open set in an affine space in which the linear part is a complex vector space defined over ℝ\mathbb{R}, and so it has an even dimension. The set of all such manifolds that arise from orbit closures is countable, and finite in the case of such submanifolds arising from marking pairs of points that are also blocked with blocking cardinality n≥0n\geq 0 (as shown in [LMW16] and cited in Proposition 2.7).

Lemma 2.9.

Let MM a translation surface obtained by the unfolding of a rational polygon with connected interior QQ, k≥0k\geq 0 an integer and let ℳQ,k​=def​{(x,y)∈M^2:(π⁡(x),π⁡(y))∈𝒬k}\mathcal{M}_{Q,k}\overset{\textup{{def}}}{=}\{(x,y)\in\widehat{M}^{2}:(\pi(x),\pi(y))\in\mathcal{Q}_{k}\} the set of pairs of points that are lifts of 𝒬k\mathcal{Q}_{k}. If ℳ|Γ|​k⊊M^2\mathcal{M}_{|\Gamma|k}\subsetneq\widehat{M}^{2} then for any S⊂ℳ|Γ|​kS\subset\mathcal{M}_{|\Gamma|k} a translation surface affinely embedded in M^2\widehat{M}^{2}, the intersection of ℳQ,k\mathcal{M}_{Q,k} with SS is finite.

Proof.

First note that by Lemma 2.3, ℳQ,k⊂ℳ|Γ|​k\mathcal{M}_{Q,k}\subset\mathcal{M}_{|\Gamma|k}. Assume ℳ|Γ|​k⊊M^2\mathcal{M}_{|\Gamma|k}\subsetneq\widehat{M}^{2}. By Proposition 2.7 it is a finite union of 00-manifolds and 22-dimensional linear submanifolds which are either of the form F×MF\times M or M×FM\times F for some finite F⊂MF\subset M, or translation surfaces affinely embedded in M^2\widehat{M}^{2}. Let S⊂ℳ|Γ|​kS\subset\mathcal{M}_{|\Gamma|k} be a translation surface affinely embedded in M^2\widehat{M}^{2} and assume by contradiction that ℳQ,k∩S\mathcal{M}_{Q,k}\cap S is infinite. In the complex coordinates of M^2\widehat{M}^{2}, a suitable neighborhood UU of SS is a set of solutions for a linear equation of the form a​x+b​y=uax+by=u for nonzero a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}, with xx a point in the first component and yy a point in the second component of M^2\widehat{M}^{2}. UU can be taken to be an open ball that contains infinitely many elements of ℳQ,k\mathcal{M}_{Q,k}. Without loss of generality, QQ is such that one of its edges is horizontal (the blocking property as well as QQ being a rational polygon would persist if we rotate QQ and its unfolding). By the unfolding process, the horizontal reflection RhR_{h} is an element of Γ\Gamma. Consider the action of Γ2\Gamma^{2} on the product space M^2\widehat{M}^{2}, under which ℳQ,k\mathcal{M}_{Q,k} is invariant (Lemma 2.4). By Lemma 2.3 We have that (Rh,1Γ)​(ℳQ,k∩U)(R_{h},{1_{\Gamma}})(\mathcal{M}_{Q,k}\cap U) is also a subset of ℳ|Γ|​k\mathcal{M}_{|\Gamma|k}. Proposition 2.10 (Apisa, Wright [AW17], Corollary 3.8).

A point x∈M∖Σx\in M\setminus\Sigma on a translation surface MM that is not a branched cover of the torus, is finitely blocked from only finitely many other points.

Corollary 2.11.

If MM is not a torus cover, then for every integer k≥0k\geq 0, ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} is the union of a finite set and finitely many translation surfaces affinely embedded in M^2\widehat{M}^{2}.

Proof.

By Proposition 2.10, for every x∈M∖Σx\in M\setminus\Sigma the set {y∈M∖Σ:B​C​(x,y)≤k}\{y\in M\setminus\Sigma:BC(x,y)\leq k\} is finite hence ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} does not coincide with M^2\widehat{M}^{2} so by Proposition 2.7 it is a finite union of 00 and 22-dimensional submanifolds of the kinds described in this proposition. Again, by Proposition 2.10, ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} cannot contain any set of the form {x}×M\{x\}\times M or M×{x}M\times\{x\} for any xx, so the only 22-dimensional manifolds that comprise the union are translation surfaces affinely embedded in M^2\widehat{M}^{2}. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

First we note that for n≥0n\geq 0 we have by Lemma 2.3 that the lift of 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n}, denoted ℳQ,n\mathcal{M}_{Q,n} is a subset of ℳ|Γ|​n\mathcal{M}_{|\Gamma|n}, and that it is sufficient to show that ℳQ,n\mathcal{M}_{Q,n} is finite as then 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} must be finite as a projection of a finite set. (i)(i): In the case of illumination, we can always find a pair of close enough points so that they illuminate each other, hence ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} cannot coincide with M^2\widehat{M}^{2}. We can then consider ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} as a finite union of 00 and 22-dimensional submanifolds, and observe that ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} cannot contain any submanifolds of the form F×MF\times M or M×FM\times F for some finite F⊂MF\subset M as these submanifolds contain pairs of close enough points that illuminate each other. By Lemma 2.9, ℳQ,n\mathcal{M}_{Q,n} has a finite intersection with each of the finitely many possible submanifolds of ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} which are translation surfaces affinely embedded in M^2\widehat{M}^{2}, so ℳQ,n\mathcal{M}_{Q,n} must be finite and hence 𝒬0\mathcal{Q}_{0} is finite. In other words, there are only finitely many pairs of points on the polygon QQ that do not illuminate each other. (i​i)(ii): let n>0n>0 and assume that MM is not a torus cover, then by Proposition 2.10, ℳ|Γ|​n\mathcal{M}_{|\Gamma|n} does not coincide with M^2\widehat{M}^{2} and by Corollary 2.11 it is the union of a finite set and finitely many translation surfaces affinely embedded in M^2\widehat{M}^{2}. Now similarly, by Lemma 2.9 ℳQ,n\mathcal{M}_{Q,n} has a finite intersection with any translation surface affinely embedded in M^2\widehat{M}^{2} and hence it is finite and so is 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n}. The ”only if” direction is evident from the result by Lelièvre, Monteil and Weiss, that MM is a torus cover if and only if for some k≥0k\geq 0, ℳk=M^2\mathcal{M}_{k}=\widehat{M}^{2} ([LMW16], Theorem 1). Note that this statement in [LMW16] holds for general translation surfaces, that are not necessarily constructed by unfolding a rational polygon. In our case, condition 2 in Lemma 2.3 is satisfied for infinitely many distinct A,B∈QA,B\in Q, hence 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} is infinite. Note that Lemma 2.3 uses a general construction of a blocking set to derive blocking of points A,BA,B in the polygon from blocking in the preimages of AA and BB on the surface, while in the special case of ramified covers of the torus, [LMW16] shows explicit constructions that rely on midpoints of trajectories between a pair of points on the torus, which can be lifted to a blocking set for pairs of points in the cover and provide a more explicit build of blocking sets for 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n}. ∎

3 A little more about illumination

The two points on the polygon in Figure 1 do not illuminate each other. This polygon’s construction is made to work with the same construction theorem that bases the proof of [Tok95]’s 2626-gon. In essence, a polygon QQ is taken such that the 45​9​45​9​9045\mhyphen 45\mhyphen 90 triangle △​A​B​C\triangle ABC tiles it by successive reflections in a way that the points corresponding to BB and CC are all vertices of QQ, and there is a pair of points in the interior of QQ that folds down to AA. Any trajectory on the polygon connecting this pair of points would have to fold down to a trajectory on the triangle that returns to AA, but such trajectories do not exist (see [Tok95] §3, Lemma 3.1).

The following lemma extends a lemma by Tokarsky ([Tok95] Lemma 4.1) which is used to construct a more general family of polygons with a pair of points that do not illuminate each other. The above-mentioned result that no trajectory returns to an acute angle in the isosceles triangle can also be derived from this lemma.

Lemma 3.1.

Let QQ be a triangle △​A​B​C\triangle ABC with angles ∠​A\angle{A} of size π/n\pi/n and ∠​B\angle{B} of size m​π/nm\pi/n for some even nn and a positive integer m<n−1m<n-1, then there is no billiard trajectory in QQ from AA coming back to AA.

Proof.

Assume by contradiction that a billiard trajectory α⁡(t)\alpha(t) from A to A exists. We may assume that α⁡(0)=A\alpha(0)=A and apply a suitable rotation so that △​A​B​C\triangle{ABC} is aligned horizontally as in Figure 2. Let Ref​(θ)\text{Ref}(\theta) denote the reflection about a line through the origin which makes an angle of θ\theta with the XX-axis and Rot​(θ)\text{Rot}(\theta) the planar rotation by an angle of θ\theta. We can take the dihedral group for the billiard in △​A​B​C\triangle ABC to be

Γ=⟨Ref​(πn),Ref​(0),Ref​(m​πn)⟩\Gamma=\langle\text{Ref}(\frac{\pi}{n})\penalty\ ,\penalty\ \text{Ref}(0)\penalty\ ,\penalty\ \text{Ref}(\frac{m\pi}{n})\rangle

By multiplying the corresponding orthogonal matrices we have Ref​(πn)​Ref​(0)=Rot​(2​πn)\text{Ref}(\frac{\pi}{n})\text{Ref}(0)=\text{Rot}(\frac{2\pi}{n}) and (Rot​(2​πn))m−1​Ref​(πn)=Ref​(m​πn)(\text{Rot}(\frac{2\pi}{n}))^{m-1}\text{Ref}(\frac{\pi}{n})=\text{Ref}(\frac{m\pi}{n}), so the dihedral group is in fact the symmetry group of the regular nn-gon:

Γ=⟨Ref​(πn),Rot​(2​πn)⟩≃Dn\Gamma=\langle\text{Ref}(\frac{\pi}{n})\penalty\ ,\penalty\ \text{Rot}(\frac{2\pi}{n})\rangle\simeq D_{n}

Consider the 2​n2n copies of the triangle, unfolded about the vertex AA to form a polygon as in Figure 3. Glued according to the unfolding construction, this is the translation surface associated with QQ. The vertex AA with angle π/n\pi/n unfolds to a removable singularity, considered to be situated at the origin OO. Let α~​(t)\widetilde{\alpha}(t) be a lift of α⁡(t)\alpha(t) such that for small enough ε\varepsilon, every 0<t<ε0<t<\varepsilon has α⁡(t)∈Q(1Γ)\alpha(t)\in Q_{(1_{\Gamma})}. Note that at time t=0t=0, α~​(t)\widetilde{\alpha}(t) traverses between Q(1Γ)Q_{(1_{\Gamma})} and the copy of QQ rotated by π\pi, that is Q(τ)Q_{(\tau)} with τ=(Rot​(2​π/n))n/2∈Γ\tau={(\text{Rot}(2\pi/n))}^{n/2}\in\Gamma being the element of rotation by π\pi. Now clearly for 0≤t≤ε0\leq t\leq\varepsilon we have α~​(t)=τ​α~​(−t)\widetilde{\alpha}(t)=\tau\widetilde{\alpha}(-t). This symmetry can be extended so that for all 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T, α~​(t)=τ​α~​(−t)\widetilde{\alpha}(t)=\tau\widetilde{\alpha}(-t) with TT denoting the minimal period time of α~​(t)\widetilde{\alpha}(t) as a closed geodesic on a translation surface.
Now observe that for the middle points we have α~(T/2)=α~(−T/2)\widetilde{\alpha}(T/2)=\widetilde{\alpha}(-T/2) but also α~(T/2)=τα~(−T/2)\widetilde{\alpha}(T/2)=\tau\widetilde{\alpha}(-T/2), so α~​(T/2)\widetilde{\alpha}(T/2) is fixed under τ\tau. As Γ\Gamma acts freely on π−1​(i​n​t​(Q))\pi^{-1}(int(Q)), α~​(T/2)\widetilde{\alpha}(T/2) cannot be a lift of an interior point of QQ, so it is a lift of a boundary point. By construction, each lift of a point interior to an edge of QQ is fixed by a single reflection element of Γ\Gamma, so α~​(T/2)\widetilde{\alpha}(T/2) must be a singularity (possibly a removable singularity in case the corresponding vertex is π/k\pi/k for some integer kk). This is a contradiction to α~​(t)\widetilde{\alpha}(t) being a closed geodesic avoiding singularities (in case α~​(T/2)≠O\widetilde{\alpha}(T/2)\neq O), or to TT being the minimal period (in case α~​(T/2)=O\widetilde{\alpha}(T/2)=O).
